A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same geometric hallucination study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite renaming and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original response-generation experiments, human annotation validation, geometric analyses, label-propagation results, and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds CoQA experiments, external baselines, classifier and encoder ablations, and further annotation and sensitivity analyses.

M1.justification: The regularized Fisher projection and Wasserstein-based label-assignment procedure remain unchanged in Sections 3.3–3.4. APORIA and APORIA-LP name the existing framework and propagator; alternative encoders and classifiers are evaluated as ablations rather than incorporated into a revised method.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates the authors' time-sensitive factual-question corpus, renamed SOCRATES-300K in v3 without changing its coverage. v3 Appendix D adds CoQA-89K, generated from 199 conversational question-answer prompts, substantially extending evaluation beyond the original temporal-event questions.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated SelfCheckGPT (NLI), SemanticEntropy, and INSIDE comparisons in Table 4, plus an INSIDE re-execution on CoQA. Appendix E adds Euclidean/cosine centroid classifiers, Linear Regression, SVM, and kNN-5. The earlier Fisher-versus-UMAP/wPCA/EP comparison remains in Appendix F.

E3.justification: The original generation settings and 2/3–1/3 evaluation splits remain. New protocols include CoQA generation with three models, 150 responses per prompt, temperature 0.5, top-p 0.99, top-k 5, and ROUGE-L-based labels. External baselines introduce response subsampling, NLI clustering, and an SBERT-based INSIDE proxy; classifier ablations compare Fisher and original embedding spaces.

E4.justification: v3 adds encoder ablations, Fisher-direction similarity across prompts/models, response-set-size sensitivity, and classifier-replacement controls. Appendix A.2 adds disagreement categories and examples, inspection of 441 unknown responses, and a Gemini judge comparison. The existing stemming analysis also gains an embedding-similarity check. These investigate several previously untested robustness and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: Existing split counts, training subsampling, mean/std reporting, and 100-permutation null comparisons are retained. The new response-set-size analysis specifies 20 repeated subsamples and reports Wasserstein permutation-significance rates separately from merely exceeding the mean null distance (Figure 7). This extends statistical assessment without establishing additional runs for the original experiments.

E6.justification: Matched original tables retain their values, including 87.2% accuracy and 90.7% F1 in Table 2. Substantial new results include CoQA averages of 98.1% accuracy and 97.1% F1 under its distinct settings (Table 12). Table 13 newly reports Fisher-space F1 of 91.4% for Linear Regression versus 90.5% for APORIA-LP, alongside new baseline, robustness, and annotation findings.

T1.justification: The Wasserstein definition, Fisher objective, regularized scatter matrix, projection, and classification rule are retained. Neither the renamed framework nor the additional empirical analyses introduce a new formal derivation, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The central geometric-asymmetry and label-efficiency contributions remain. v3 explicitly adds generation and reproduction code to its release contribution. Its conclusion replaces the claim of F1 above 90% 'across all models' with F1 above 90% on SOCRATES-300K, although the abstract retains broader wording.

C2.justification: v3 interprets Fisher-direction differences as evidence of prompt-specific geometry and explains encoder/judge robustness and CoQA behavior. Appendix E explicitly prioritizes the structural finding over the propagator because standard classifiers perform similarly. It also adds interpretations of conservative annotation errors, limited small-sample significance, and the restricted comparability of external detector baselines.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a dataset DOI and repository references for dataset generation and result reproduction, whereas v1 only announces dataset release. It also documents baseline adaptations, CoQA model identifiers and generation/labeling settings, and the stratified selection of the existing human-validation sample. These substantially expand reproducibility information; linked resources were not accessed.

R1.justification: Related work adds INSIDE and expands its relationship to SemanticEntropy, SelfCheckGPT, and the dataset motivation. New citations also support CoQA, ROUGE, and broader background. The overall research positioning remains; changes to HEMM's author ordering and several publication records concern already-cited works.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract, introduces consistent framework/dataset names, adds descriptive paragraph headings, and reorganizes appendix subsections. It also corrects the running header and updates author/publication information. The main six-section narrative and most existing methodological exposition remain, making the editorial reworking more limited than the experimental expansion.

P2.justification: v3 adds six substantive tables covering encoders, detectors, annotation disagreements, CoQA, and classifiers, plus new response-size and CoQA figures. Figure 9 augments the retained training-size plot with numerical summaries, and annotation examples receive boxed displays. Existing plots and tables are largely retained and relocated, rather than replaced with new results.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited validation of dataset generality, encoder dependence, annotation reliability, and classifier necessity. The CoQA evaluation and added controls clarify both the geometric finding and its boundaries, while explicit resource references improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh shortcomings: detector comparisons remain proxies, Table 3's default-encoder F1 is unexplained relative to Table 2, and Table 11 contains inconsistent totals. The improvement rests on stronger scrutiny and broader evidence, rather than higher reported scores alone.
